ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2020-01-15
Provider: Dr. Aisha Patel, MD
Department: Emergency Medicine
Visit Type: ed

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Yellowing of the skin

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a male neonate with congenital rubella syndrome and cephalohematoma who presents to the Emergency Department following evaluations for a murmur and head swelling. He is brought by his mother due to yellowing of the skin. The mother is O positive and reports a healthy pregnancy and an uncomplicated vaginal delivery at term. She mentions that the baby has been breastfeeding well but seems more sleepy than her previous child.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Congenital rubella syndrome (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Cephalohematoma due to birth injury (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Retinoblastoma of the right eye
- Patent ductus arteriosus
- History of ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
- History of neonatal cephalohematoma

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery
- Circumcision

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Ibuprofen lysine 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 doses (PDA closure protocol)
- Furosemide 1 mg/kg PO q12h PRN (for symptomatic PDA/CHF management)

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Maternal first-trimester rubella infection (non-immune status during pregnancy)
- Maternal blood type O positive
- Paternal blood type A positive (ABO incompatibility)
- No family history of retinoblastoma or other childhood malignancies (sporadic mutation)
- No family history of congenital heart disease

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never (age inappropriate). Alcohol: None (age inappropriate). Occupation: None (pediatric patient).

VITAL SIGNS:
Vital signs are within normal limits.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
On examination, the infant appears jaundiced but is otherwise well.
The abdomen is soft, non-distended, with no hepatosplenomegaly.

LABORATORY DATA:
Laboratory tests reveal:

- Hemoglobin: 14 g/dL (normal for neonate)
- Total bilirubin: 18 mg/dL
- Direct bilirubin: 1.2 mg/dL
- Blood type: A positive
- Direct Coombs test: Positive

ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2020-07-15
Provider: Dr. Robert Thompson, MD
Department: Dermatology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Concerned about a persistent rash on his scalp

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a male infant with congenital rubella syndrome, retinoblastoma, and patent ductus arteriosus presenting with a persistent scalp rash. The rash appeared two weeks ago and has not improved with regular bathing. The infant is otherwise healthy and meeting all developmental milestones.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Congenital rubella syndrome (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Cephalohematoma due to birth injury (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- ABO hemolytic disease of newborn (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Patent ductus arteriosus (diagnosed 2020-02-15)
- Congenital hydrocele (diagnosed 2020-04-15)
- Retinoblastoma of the right eye
- History of ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
- History of neonatal cephalohematoma

He was born at term without complications.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery
- Circumcision

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Ibuprofen lysine 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 doses (PDA closure protocol)
- Furosemide 1 mg/kg PO q12h PRN (for symptomatic PDA/CHF management)

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
The mother denies any family history of atopic dermatitis or psoriasis.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never (age inappropriate). Alcohol: None (age inappropriate). Occupation: None (pediatric patient).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
On examination, the infant is well-appearing and afebrile. The scalp shows thick, greasy, yellowish scales, and similar lesions are noted on the eyelids and in the nasolabial folds. There is no evidence of lymphadenopathy, and the rest of the physical examination is normal.

ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2020-02-15
Provider: Dr. James Kim, MD
Department: Pediatrics
Visit Type: inpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Poor feeding and increased work of breathing

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a male infant with congenital rubella syndrome, recently evaluated for neonatal cephalohematoma and ABO hemolytic disease, who returns for ongoing care. His mother reports that he breathes rapidly even at rest and takes long pauses while feeding, often falling asleep before finishing his bottle. She also notes that his pulses feel "strong" and that his breathing seems louder when lying down.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Congenital rubella syndrome (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Cephalohematoma due to birth injury (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- ABO hemolytic disease of newborn (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Retinoblastoma of the right eye
- Patent ductus arteriosus
- History of ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
- History of neonatal cephalohematoma

The baby was born full-term and had normal APGAR scores. He has not had any cyanosis or fever.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery
- Circumcision

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Ibuprofen lysine 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 doses (PDA closure protocol)
- Furosemide 1 mg/kg PO q12h PRN (for symptomatic PDA/CHF management)

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Maternal first-trimester rubella infection (non-immune status during pregnancy)
- Maternal blood type O positive
- Paternal blood type A positive (ABO incompatibility)
- No family history of retinoblastoma or other childhood malignancies (sporadic mutation)
- No family history of congenital heart disease

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never (age inappropriate). Alcohol: None (age inappropriate). Occupation: None (pediatric patient).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
Physical exam reveals a hyperdynamic precordium and bounding peripheral pulses. On auscultation, a continuous murmur is heard best at the left infraclavicular area. There are no signs of hepatomegaly or peripheral cyanosis.

OTHER STUDIES:
Cardiac catheterization is performed to further evaluate the suspected lesion, and oxygen saturation values are shown in the image.

ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2020-04-15
Provider: Dr. Emily Johnson, MD
Department: Urology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Noticing a swelling in his right scrotum

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The infant returns for urologic evaluation with a history of congenital rubella syndrome, retinoblastoma, patent ductus arteriosus, and prior neonatal cephalohematoma and ABO hemolytic disease. The parents report that the swelling seems to be painless, as the infant does not cry or show signs of discomfort when the area is touched. The infant has been feeding well and has had no fever or vomiting. His birth history is unremarkable, and he was born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery without complications.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Congenital rubella syndrome (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Cephalohematoma due to birth injury (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- ABO hemolytic disease of newborn (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Patent ductus arteriosus (diagnosed 2020-02-15)
- Retinoblastoma of the right eye
- History of ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
- History of neonatal cephalohematoma

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery
- Circumcision

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Ibuprofen lysine 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 doses (PDA closure protocol)
- Furosemide 1 mg/kg PO q12h PRN (for symptomatic PDA/CHF management)

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Maternal first-trimester rubella infection (non-immune status during pregnancy)
- Maternal blood type O positive
- Paternal blood type A positive (ABO incompatibility)
- No family history of retinoblastoma or other childhood malignancies (sporadic mutation)
- No family history of congenital heart disease

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never (age inappropriate). Alcohol: None (age inappropriate). Occupation: None (pediatric patient).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
On physical examination, the pediatrician observes a non-tender, smooth, and swollen right hemiscrotum. The left scrotum appears normal. Transillumination of the right scrotum reveals a red glow. The abdomen is soft and non-distended, with no palpable masses. The rest of the physical examination is within normal limits.
